entry: Iranian empire, one of the largest and longest-lasting in the country's history, ruled by the [[Safavid dynasty]] from 1501 to 1736. Some historians date its fall to 1722, when [[Isfahan]] fell to the Afghans. [[Ismail I|Shah Ismail I]] made Twelver Shi'ism the official religion, a turning point in the history of Islam, and the empire is often considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. At its height it controlled present-day [[Iran]], [[Azerbaijan]] and [[Armenia]], eastern Georgia and Iraq, as well as parts of Turkey and Syria. The Safavids also patronized the arts, and their architecture remains a legacy.

Ruling dynasty of [[Iran]] from 1501 to 1736, of Kurdish origin and both Persian- and Turkish-speaking. The dynasty arose from the Safavid Sufi order, based in Ardabil in the [[Azerbaijan]] region. Under [[Ismail I|Shah Ismail I]] it made Twelver Shi'a Islam the official religion of the Persian Empire, one of the most important turning points in the history of Islam. The Safavids were the first native dynasty since the [[Sasanian Empire]] to establish a national state officially known as Iran, and their rule is often considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. Their claim to legitimacy rested on descent from [[Ali]], regarded by the Shi'a as the first Imam. Although the dynasty ended in 1736, it revived Iran as an economic stronghold between East and West and left a legacy in architecture and the fine arts.

State of being protected from harm or other danger. The word entered the [[English language]] in the 14th century, from Latin salvus, meaning uninjured or in good health. Safety can also refer to the control of recognized hazards to achieve an acceptable level of risk. There is no universally accepted definition: it may be described as the absence of risk and adverse incidents, or as the capacity to defend against adverse events and mitigate their effects. The [[Oxford English Dictionary]] defines it as "freedom from danger and risks." As an outcome, safety is an acceptable history of adverse events; as a target, it involves proactive planning to minimize risk; and as an ongoing process, it protects people, property and the environment when incidents occur. [[Engineering|Safety engineering]] applies scientific principles to identify and control dangers across the life of a system.

Five-category scale that classifies hurricanes by their sustained winds. Developed in 1971 by engineer Herbert Saffir and meteorologist Robert Simpson, it was introduced to the public in 1973. A hurricane must have one-minute sustained winds of at least 74 mph (64 kn, 119 km/h), and Category 5 storms have winds of at least 157 mph (137 kn, 252 km/h). The scale measures wind only and does not account for rain or storm surge, a criticism its defenders answer by citing its simplicity. It applies officially to hurricanes in the Atlantic and northern Pacific east of the [[International Date Line]].

Spice made from the dried stigmas and styles of the autumn-blooming flower Crocus sativus, the saffron crocus. Saffron is used mainly as a food seasoning and [[Dye|colorant]]. Its taste and aroma come from the phytochemicals picrocrocin and safranal, and the [[Carotenoid|carotenoid]] pigment crocin gives dishes and textiles a golden-yellow hue. The crocus is sterile and cannot produce viable seeds, so humans have propagated it across much of [[Eurasia]]. It originated in the Khorasan region of northeastern [[Iran]], and its recorded history begins with a 7th-century BC Assyrian botanical treatise. Harvesting is labor-intensive, and premium saffron regularly exceeds US$5,000 per kilogram. Saffron is an essential ingredient in Persian cuisine and has also been used in [[Traditional medicine]], dyeing, perfumery and religious [[Ritual|rituals]].

Prose story or history composed in [[Iceland]] and, to a lesser extent, elsewhere in [[Scandinavia]]. Sagas originated in the [[Middle Ages]] and were written in the vernacular, Old Norse and its later descendants, primarily Icelandic, rather than in [[Latin]], the dominant language of medieval European history-writing. Their subjects range from pre-Christian Scandinavian legends and saints to Scandinavian kings, contemporary Icelandic politics and chivalric romances. The most famous type is the sagas of Icelanders, which feature Viking voyages, migration to Iceland and feuds between Icelandic families, usually set from the settlement of Iceland in the 870s to a generation or two after its conversion to Christianity in 1000. Kings' sagas, composed in the 12th to 14th centuries, chronicle the lives of Scandinavian kings; Heimskringla, probably compiled by [[Snorri Sturluson]], is a pre-eminent example. Though written in prose, sagas often include [[Epic poetry|verse]] in alliterative form.

[[Supermassive black hole]] at the [[Galactic Center]] of the [[Milky Way]], about 27,000 light-years from Earth. It was discovered in 1974 by Bruce Balick and Robert L. Brown, who identified it as a compact radio source. Observations of stars orbiting it, particularly the star S2, indicate a mass of 4.297±0.012 million [[Solar mass|solar masses]]. In May 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of the accretion disk around its [[Event horizon]], the second confirmed image of a black hole after that of [[Messier 87]] in 2019. Its radio and infrared emissions come from gas and dust heated to millions of degrees as it falls in. Dust and gas block visible light, with 25 magnitudes of extinction. In 2020 Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez each received a quarter-share of the Nobel Prize in Physics for showing that it is a supermassive compact object.

Zodiac constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere, whose name is Latin for archer. It lies between [[Scorpius]] and [[Ophiuchus]] and is one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer [[Ptolemy]] and one of the 88 modern constellations. It is commonly depicted as a centaur drawing a bow. The center of the [[Milky Way]] lies in its westernmost part. Its brightest stars form a teapot-shaped asterism, and the constellation is a prominent feature of the northern summer sky.

Roman Catholic basilica under construction since 1882 in [[Barcelona]], Spain, designed by [[Antoni Gaudí]], who combined Gothic and curvilinear [[Art Nouveau]] forms. Construction began on March 19, 1882, under Francisco de Paula del Villar. In 1883 Gaudí took over as chief architect and devoted the rest of his life to the project; at his death in 1926 less than a quarter of it was complete. Relying solely on private donations, work was interrupted by the [[Spanish Civil War]] in 1936, when anarchists set fire to the crypt and partly destroyed Gaudí's original plans. Construction resumed in the 1950s, and computer-aided design and computer numerical control have since sped progress. The central Tower of Jesus Christ reached structural completion on February 20, 2026, and was blessed by Pope Leo XIV on June 10, 2026. At 172.5 m (566 ft), the tower makes the basilica the world's tallest church. Parts of the building were declared a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]] in 2005.

Biogeographical region of semi-arid savanna in Africa, forming a transition zone between the [[Sahara]] to the north and the more humid Sudanian savannas to the south. The name derives from Arabic sāḥil, meaning "coast, shore," a figurative reference to the southern edge of the Sahara. The region stretches about 5,900 km from the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the [[Red Sea]] and covers 3,053,200 square kilometers. Although it lies in the tropics, its hot semi-arid climate is not tropical. Rainfall varies from about 100–200 mm in the north to 700–1,000 mm in the south. Vegetation is mainly grassland and savanna, with [[Acacia]] the dominant tree. The population was approximately 80 million in 2018, and since the 2010s coups, insurgencies and foreign interventions have led to the region being called the Coup Belt.

Partially recognized state in the western [[Maghreb]] that claims sovereignty over [[Western Sahara]] but controls only its easternmost portion. It was proclaimed by the Polisario Front on February 27, 1976, in Bir Lehlou. Morocco occupies the rest of the disputed territory and calls it its Southern Provinces. The republic is a full member of the [[African Union]] but not of the [[Arab League]], and its administration is based in refugee camps near Tindouf, Algeria. The United Nations considers the Polisario Front the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi people.

Indian spiritual master and saint revered by both Hindu and Muslim devotees. He preached the realization of the self, love, forgiveness, charity and devotion to God and guru, and he condemned discrimination based on religion or [[Caste|caste]]. He lived in a [[Mosque|mosque]] in Shirdi, [[Maharashtra]], which he named Dwarakamayi, and he practiced both Hindu and Muslim rituals. His Hindu devotees regarded him as an incarnation of the deity Dattatreya, according to the hagiography Shri Sai Satcharita, written shortly after his death. His real name and origins are unknown.

Indian actor and film producer who works primarily in Hindi films. Born in [[New Delhi]], he is the son of actress [[Sharmila Tagore]] and cricketer Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi. He made his acting debut in Parampara (1993) and earned critical acclaim for Dil Chahta Hai (2001), Ek Hasina Thi (2004) and Omkara (2006), in which he played Iago. He headlined [[Netflix]]'s first original Indian series, Sacred Games (2018–2019). Khan received the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian award, in 2010. He owns the production companies Illuminati Films and Black Knight Films and was married to [[Kareena Kapoor]] after his first marriage to Amrita Singh.

Tensile structure of fabric or other membrane material that uses wind power to propel sailing craft. Sails are made from canvas or polyester cloth, laminated membranes or bonded filaments, usually in a three- or four-sided shape. They produce propulsive force through [[Lift (force)|lift]] and [[Drag (physics)|drag]], depending on their angle of attack to the apparent wind, and on points of sail close to the wind they act as an airfoil. Sails are attached to a mast, boom or other spar, raised by a halyard and angled to the wind by a sheet, and battens can extend the trailing edge. There are two main rig types: the square rig, with yards set perpendicular to the keel, and the fore-and-aft rig, with sails set along the keel. Modern sails often use high-performance materials such as [[Kevlar]] and Dyneema. The origin of the sail is unknown, and many do not consider sails to have been used before the 5th millennium BCE.

Propulsion of a vehicle by wind power. Sailing uses wind acting on [[Sail|sails]], wing sails or kites to propel a craft on water, on ice or on land over a chosen course. From prehistory until the second half of the 19th century, sailing craft were the main means of maritime trade and transport, and the gun-armed sailing warships of the Age of Sail dominated navies. Steam gradually replaced sail over the late 19th century, as steamships ran scheduled services at higher speeds and gained fuel economy. In the 21st century most sailing is recreation or [[Sailing (sport)|sport]], divided into racing and cruising. Sailing relies on the lift and drag generated by the sails, resisted by the hull, keel and rudder, which lets a boat sail both upwind and downwind but not too close into the wind. It was probably invented independently in Island Southeast Asia and the Mediterranean, possibly including the [[Nile]] and the Guayaquil River in Ecuador.

Sea-going vessel that uses sails mounted on masts to harness wind power. Sailing ships carried square-rigged or fore-and-aft sails, or a combination of both in barques, barquentines and brigantines. Early sailing ships were used on rivers and coasts in [[Ancient Egypt]] and the Mediterranean. The [[Austronesian peoples]] developed catamaran and outrigger hulls and the crab-claw sail, which enabled their expansion beginning in Taiwan c. 3000 BC across the islands of the Indo-Pacific. European ships with square rigs became prevalent during the [[Age of Discovery]], when they crossed oceans between continents. By the 1880s, ships with triple-expansion steam engines could compete with sail on all major routes, though commercial sail continued into the 20th century, with the last ceasing to trade by c. 1960.

Competitive sport in which sailing craft race in fleets, in pairs or in teams. Races are held on closed courses or point to point, in sheltered waters, along coasts or on the open ocean, and are sanctioned by federations and yacht clubs. A competition among multiple vessels is a regatta, made up of several races, and the crew that performs best over the series is the overall winner. In fleet racing a race can include anywhere from four boats to hundreds, and a regatta must comprise at least three races to count. Match racing pits two boats against each other, with the aim of finishing ahead of the opponent rather than sailing as fast as possible. Team racing usually involves two teams of three boats each, and the team that scores ten or fewer points wins. The Racing Rules of Sailing govern yacht racing, windsurfing, kitesurfing and other racing around a course. The Barcolana regatta in Italy holds the Guinness World Record for the largest sailing race, with 2,689 boats and over 16,000 sailors at the starting line.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series written and illustrated by Naoko Takeuchi. Serialized in the shōjo magazine Nakayoshi from 1991 to 1997, it follows Usagi Tsukino, a schoolgirl in [[Tokyo]] who transforms into a magical heroine to protect the [[Solar System]] from villains. A Toei Animation anime series, broadcast in Japan from 1992 to 1997, helped popularize anime in the [[Western world]], particularly in the United States. The manga has sold over 46 million copies worldwide, making it one of the best-selling shōjo manga series of all time.

Person recognized as having an exceptional degree of holiness, likeness or closeness to God. In Christian belief, saints are recognized through canonization in the [[Catholic Church]] or glorification in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]]; some nonconformist denominations, such as the Plymouth Brethren, use the term for any holy Christian. The word derives from [[Latin]] sanctus, meaning "holy" or "consecrated," and entered English through Old French and [[Middle English]]. Historians of religion also apply the term to holy figures in other faiths, including the Hindu rishi, the Islamic walī and the Buddhist arhat. Veneration of saints is distinct from [[Worship|worship]], which is reserved for God, and may involve relics, images and novenas. In the Catholic Church, canonization examines a person's life, virtues and the miracles attributed to their intercession.

Overseas collectivity of France in the Leeward Islands of the northeastern Caribbean. A volcanic island of about 25 square kilometers, it had a population of 10,660 at the January 2023 census. [[Christopher Columbus]] named it in 1493 in honor of Bartholomew the Apostle. After nearly a century as a [[Sweden|Swedish]] colony, it returned to French rule after an 1877 referendum. In 2003 the island voted to secede from [[Guadeloupe]] and form a separate overseas collectivity. Its capital, Gustavia, has the main harbor, and the island is a luxury tourist destination during the winter holiday season.

Early Christian martyr and soldier venerated as a saint, sentenced to death during the Diocletianic Persecution. According to tradition he was of Cappadocian Greek origin and a member of the Praetorian Guard of Roman emperor [[Diocletian]], who condemned him for refusing to recant his Christian faith. He became one of the most venerated saints in [[Christianity]] and, since the [[Crusades]], especially a military saint. He is immortalized in the legend of Saint George and the Dragon and is one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers in Roman Catholicism. His feast day, April 23, is traditionally celebrated, and Portugal, England, Bulgaria, Georgia, Ukraine and Malta are among the countries that have claimed him as patron. Little is known of his life, and early sources conflict. A sarcophagus traditionally believed to hold his relics is in the Church of Saint George in Lydda, now Lod in Israel.

Volcanic island in the South Atlantic Ocean, part of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. It had a population of 4,439 at the 2021 census. It was named after Helena of Constantinople, and tradition holds that Portuguese explorers sighted it in 1502. For about four centuries it was a stopover for ships sailing around Africa, before the opening of the [[Suez Canal]] in 1869. The island is known as the site of the second exile of [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]], who was held there from his defeat at the [[Battle of Waterloo]] in 1815 until his death six years later.

Two-island federation in the [[Lesser Antilles]] of the Caribbean, the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere by area and population. It covers 261 square kilometers and has roughly 48,000 inhabitants. The capital, Basseterre, is on the larger island of Saint Kitts, and Nevis lies about 3 km to the southeast across the Narrows. Saint Kitts was home to the first British and French Caribbean colonies. The federation became an associated state of the [[United Kingdom]] in 1964 and gained independence in 1983, the most recent British territory in the Caribbean to do so. [[Charles III]] is king and [[Head of state|head of state]]. Its economy has shifted from sugar to tourism, which contributes over 60% of GDP through cruise ship visits and luxury resorts.

Island country in the Windward Islands of the [[Lesser Antilles]] in the eastern Caribbean. Its capital and largest city is Castries, and it covers 617 square kilometers. It had an officially estimated population of over 184,100 in mid-2023. England and France fought 14 times for control of the island, and the British took complete control in 1814, shortly after the victory over French Emperor Napoleon I. Because it changed hands so often, it was known as the "Helen of the West" after [[Helen of Troy]]. Representative government was introduced in 1924 and universal suffrage in 1951. Saint Lucia became independent on February 22, 1979, while remaining a Commonwealth realm. It is a member of the [[United Nations]], the [[Organization of American States]], the [[World Trade Organization]] and CARICOM, and tourism drives its economy.

Caribbean island in the Leeward Islands of the [[Lesser Antilles]], divided between [[France]] and the [[Kingdom of the Netherlands]]. Since the 1648 Treaty of Concordia the 87-square-kilometer island has been divided roughly 60:40 between the French collectivity of Saint-Martin, 53 square kilometers, and the Dutch [[Sint Maarten]], 34 square kilometers. The Dutch side is more populous, and the island had 73,777 inhabitants on January 1, 2019. Only the French part belongs to the [[European Union]]. The highest hilltop is Pic Paradis, at 424 m. Hurricane Irma devastated the island in September 2017, and Princess Juliana International Airport is its main airport.
